title_en: The Critic Who Came to Dinner
description_ru: Владелец ресторана узнаёт грозного критика и пытается его умаслить, а критик делает вид, что никого не знает. Язвительный диалог о еде, самолюбии и соли.
text:
Lucien: Madame Ferrand! What an unexpected honour. May I say that your table by the window has been waiting for you since about, oh, nine o'clock this morning, when a very small bird told me you had a reservation under the name of Mrs. Smith.
Dorothea: I do not know any Mrs. Smith, and I certainly do not know any small birds. I am simply a hungry woman in a sensible coat. I would be obliged if you would stop looking at me as though I were a tax inspector who had come to inspect your drains.

Lucien: Of course, of course. A hungry woman. We have so many of those, and we treat them all identically, with the same warm and entirely spontaneous hospitality. Might I suggest, purely as a friend, that you try tonight's special? A trio of line-caught sea bass, with a foam of lemon verbena and the faintest breath of smoked salt.
Dorothea: A foam. How very brave of the sea bass. I think I should prefer something that has not been aerated. Tell me, what do you recommend that is made of an ingredient and then left alone?

Lucien: Ah, a purist. In that case, the lamb. It has been slow-cooked for fourteen hours, rested, and then treated with the respect that is due to an animal that has led a blameless life on a Welsh hillside. It is accompanied by a single carrot, for which I will not apologise, since it is the most distinguished carrot in the county.
Dorothea: One carrot. Admirable restraint. Bring me the lamb, and a glass of something red that does not announce itself to the room. And Monsieur Lucien, you may go and stand behind the kitchen door now. I shall be perfectly capable of eating without a chaperone.

Lucien: Naturally. I shall be nowhere. I shall be a small, discreet, inconspicuous cloud of nothing. Though, should you require anything, a napkin, a second fork, or some forgiveness, I will be hovering, invisibly, beside the bread.
Dorothea: How very reassuring. Go.

Lucien: Madame, forgive me, I am back so soon. Is the lamb to your satisfaction? I could not help noticing that you have turned the plate a quarter turn clockwise. Chefs are sensitive to these things. It is rather like watching a stranger straighten a painting in your house.
Dorothea: I turned the plate because the carrot had been placed at an angle that I found presumptuous. The lamb, however, is excellent. It is tender, it is deep, it has the quiet confidence of a thing that does not need to be loud. I will not tell you how excellent. You would put it on the menu, and then you would become insufferable.

Lucien: I am already insufferable, Madame, it is a professional requirement. But I thank you. One does not often receive a compliment from a woman who has ended three restaurants by describing their soup as "regret in a bowl".
Dorothea: That soup deserved it. It had been made by a man who believed salt was a kind of rumour. Incidentally, Lucien, I observe that you are standing on my left side, which is the side from which waiters in this establishment seem to deliver the bad news.

Lucien: Forgive me, Madame, that is a custom of the house, and one I have long meant to abolish. The previous owner believed that bad news should be delivered from the left, because it is nearer the heart, and therefore hurts less. I can only say that I have found no evidence for the theory, but a great deal for the habit. May I at least offer you a little more of the wine? It is a Burgundy of modest ambition and impeccable manners.
Dorothea: You may pour exactly one centimetre, and you may not tell me where it was grown, who grew it, or what its grandmother thought of the weather. I have sat through lectures on terroir that lasted longer than my first marriage. Tell me instead, Lucien, why you left the grand hotel in the city to open this little place, with its eleven tables and its wobbly chairs.

Lucien: Because, Madame, in a grand hotel nobody eats the food. They eat the chandeliers, the reputation, the waiters in white gloves. I wished to cook for people who would notice if the potatoes were wrong. Which, as you have just demonstrated, includes at least one person who would notice if the potatoes were wrong in the next county.
Dorothea: That is quite a pretty speech. Did you rehearse it in the pantry, beneath my photograph?

Lucien: Madame, I have rehearsed everything in the pantry beneath your photograph. I once proposed to my wife there, by mistake, in a moment of confusion, and she accepted.
Dorothea: Then my influence is more far-reaching than I supposed.

Lucien: Madame, I am only here to ask whether you will take dessert. We have a pear tart, a chocolate pot, and a thing I would hesitate to describe as a soufflé, because it is more of an argument between egg and air. The pastry chef, I should add, is my nephew, and he is extremely nervous.
Dorothea: Then I shall have the soufflé, and I shall be kind to it. Tell your nephew that I do not bite. I merely chew thoughtfully and write devastating things afterwards. Now, as a matter of curiosity, how long did you take to recognise me tonight? I should like to know whether the staff of this restaurant are as perceptive as they are polite.

Lucien: Madame, I recognised you before you came through the door. Your photograph has been taped inside the pantry since January, with a small note beneath it saying, "If she asks for water, panic quietly". We have rehearsed. I am sorry. We are, in the end, only human, and a little afraid.
Dorothea: Good. A restaurant that is not a little afraid of its customers will soon be afraid of nothing at all, which is the beginning of bad cooking. Now go and fetch your nephew. I shall say a few words to him before the soufflé, and I give you my word that I will not be cruel.

Lucien: Madame, you are a woman of formidable generosity.
Dorothea: I am a woman who has just eaten a very good lamb. The two things are, I regret to say, often confused. Bring the bill, and bring the nephew, in that order.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: in-con-SPIC-u-ous, pre-SUMP-tu-ous, in-SUF-fer-a-ble. Безударные слоги сильно сокращаются.
Краткий звук, нечто среднее между а и ы; рот расслаблен, не округляйте губы и не произносите как о.
Звуки p, t, k в начале ударного слога произносятся с лёгким придыханием: table, tart, carrot.
Слитно: a_little_afraid звучит как a-lit-tle-fraid. Согласный в конце слова переходит к следующей гласной.

questions.question: Why is Lucien nervous about Madame Ferrand?
questions.answer: She is a feared restaurant critic.

questions.question: How did the staff recognise her?
questions.answer: Her photograph was taped inside the pantry.
